name: Maple
lede: Maple is an orangey-yellow, and the tree behind the name gives painters, violin makers and dyers three very different stories.

sections.title: An orangey-yellow
sections.body:
Paterson defines maple simply as an orangey-yellow [1]. It is listed with the yellows, near [[marigold]], [[maize]] and [[straw]] [2]. The swatch is a pale, warm gold, much lighter than the autumn leaves most people picture [3].

That is a reminder that a color named for a tree can mean wood, sap or leaf, and each is a different color [1][4].

sections.title: Maple wood and violins
sections.body: In Cremona, maple and spruce are the woods of the violin, and Finlay describes seeing a violin back cut from a single piece of maple, patterned like a tiger's coat [4]. A varnish is what lets the wood show its beauty and also shapes the tone [4].

sections.title: Autumn maples
sections.body: Gurney uses maples to teach how color works in leaves. Light passing through a leaf is a strongly chromatic yellow-green, the shaded underside differs from the shaded upper side, and direct sun on the top surface gives the highest value [5]. He also notes that Vermont draws millions of visitors each fall to see the foliage, with maples among the favorite trees [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No usable archive measurements exist for this name, so there is no painting data to quote [3].
